case40v1-growth.referral:
Kopal Solar Networks: What Is the Neighbour Actually Worth?

A case on referral programme design, rooftop solar and the difference between credit and cause.

1. Sunday night in Bhavnagar

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Ketaki Vora was still at the dining table of her flat in Kaliyabid, Bhavnagar, with two laptops open. On the left was the deck she would put to the board of Kopal Solar Networks at half past ten the next morning. On the right was the cell that had ruined her weekend: the cost of one incremental rooftop installation bought by the company's referral programme, which her data lead in Vancouver put at ₹32,480 and which the quarterly channel report, bound for the directors, put at ₹7,658.

Both came from the same customer database. Ketaki, who had joined as vice-president of growth eighteen months earlier from a lending company in Ahmedabad, had spent Saturday looking for the error that would let her delete one of them, and had not found it.

The programme was Kutumb Circle, launched in February 2025, which paid ₹4,000 to a Kopal customer whose neighbour bought a rooftop system and ₹3,000 off the invoice to the neighbour. The board had been told, repeatedly and by Ketaki, that it was the cheapest source of demand the company had. The winter selling season in Saurashtra, from Diwali through Uttarayan, opened in under four weeks, and whatever the board decided had to be priced and communicated to forty-one franchise partners before it did.

2. How Kopal got here

Kunjan Dholakia founded Kopal Solar Networks in Bhavnagar in 2019, after eleven years selling inverters and batteries across Saurashtra. The proposition was unglamorous: a 3 kW rooftop system for a middle-income household, installed end to end, with the subsidy claim filed by Kopal rather than the customer. In the year to 31 March 2026 the company commissioned 14,200 residential systems averaging 3.2 kW at an average invoice of ₹1,92,000, for revenue of ₹272.64 crore. Contribution after modules, inverter, structure, logistics and the installer's payout ran at 14 per cent, or ₹26,880 per system.

One decision from 2021 shapes everything available to Ketaki now. Short of capital and unable to hire crews fast enough, Kunjan signed exclusive territory agreements with forty-one local electrical contractors, who became Kopal Kendras — thirty-four holding one Gujarat taluka each, seven in Maharashtra and Kerala. They run to 31 March 2028 and guarantee the partner ₹11,000 per commissioned system in his territory, whoever originated the sale. Clause 9(c) bars Kopal from originating demand there through its own salaried field agents; clause 14 requires ninety days' notice before any customer-facing incentive that alters partner economics is changed. In 2021 those clauses bought a distribution network for no equity. In 2026 they mean Kopal cannot put its own people on the ground, cannot change a reward quickly, and depends on partners with their own view of whose customer a customer is.

A Singapore climate fund led a ₹168 crore Series B in March 2025; Series C diligence opens in January 2027.

3. The industry

Residential rooftop solar in India stopped being a niche in February 2024, when the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana put a central subsidy of up to ₹78,000 behind a 3 kW household system and routed applications through a national portal. Gujarat, already the leading state for residential rooftop capacity, ran its own push through the Gujarat Energy Development Agency, while the local discom, Paschim Gujarat Vij Company Limited, handled feasibility, net-metering sanction and metering in Bhavnagar district. Modules came from Waaree and Adani Solar, both Gujarat manufacturers; Tata Power Solar and Vikram Solar competed nationally; Luminous and Havells sold through the same shops that had sold Kunjan his first inverters.

The consequence was that awareness was no longer the constraint and price was no longer a secret. What households in Bhavnagar, Amreli and Botad had not resolved was trust: whether a system would be commissioned, whether the subsidy would arrive, whether the installer would return in year three. That question is answered by neighbours, not by advertising, which is the premise Kutumb Circle was built on.

Exposure beyond India is modest but real: module prices track international polysilicon markets, the Singapore investor benchmarks Kopal against Southeast Asian and European rooftop businesses whose acquisition costs run three to five times higher, and design and analytics come on contract from Berlin and Vancouver.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Kutumb Circle began as a WhatsApp scheme: a customer sent the numbers of interested neighbours to the Kendra, and if a system was commissioned, ₹4,000 arrived by UPI. By December 2025 it was credited with just under a third of all commissionings.

In January 2026, after a legal review of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, Kopal stopped accepting uploaded contact numbers and moved to a link-only design: the neighbour submits her own details and consents in her own name. Share volumes fell by about a third within six weeks. Attributed commissionings did not fall, which the growth team read as evidence that the programme had been carrying junk. Nobody asked the other question that reading implies.

In April 2026 Khyati Parekh, the chief financial officer, noticed that payouts had crossed ₹1 crore in a quarter and asked for a test. Kumud Ranade, the data science lead in Vancouver, proposed a geographic holdout. Kedar Wagle, who runs the partner network from Indore, objected that switching a reward off in a partner's taluka would be read as a breach of good faith, and that he could not do it in his strongest markets. The eight talukas eventually switched off, between 1 July and 25 August 2026, were those where his objection was weakest — which meant, though the test plan recorded it nowhere, those where Kopal's brand was oldest and word of mouth already thickest.

Kumud's results came back on 24 September as Exhibit 4. On the point estimate, the programme was buying about a fifth of the volume it was credited with. On 28 September she also found that 554 of the 1,458 payouts in the quarter, 38.0 per cent, went to households whose numbers appeared on a Kendra's own staff or family roster, and that 231 referrers accounted for 610 of the 1,458 commissioned referrals, 41.8 per cent. Neither pattern is fraud — a partner's cousin genuinely can persuade a neighbour to buy — but it is not what the board was told the programme was.

5. The people

Ketaki Vora, vice-president, growth, Bhavnagar. Owns the number and the recommendation, and has told the board for four quarters that referral is Kopal's cheapest channel. What she has not said is that she does not believe the holdout either.

Kunjan Dholakia, founder and chief executive, Bhavnagar. Believes the company was built by satisfied customers talking, and that the programme merely pays for something sacred. He has not mentioned that two of the largest Kendra partners told him privately they would take a rival's franchise if their economics thinned.

Khyati Parekh, chief financial officer, Bhavnagar. Commissioned the holdout; wants a hard quarterly ceiling and a payout tied to a commissioned, cash-collected system. She has not said that she has already modelled the Series C at a blended acquisition cost below ₹10,000.

Kedar Wagle, head of partner network, Indore. Argues that the ₹4,000 is what keeps a Kendra quoting Kopal rather than a rival brand from the same shop — a channel incentive in a customer's clothes. He resisted the holdout and got his strongest talukas excluded. He has not said that his variable pay is set on commissioned volume there.

Kavya Warrier, head of customer experience, Kochi. Runs the call centre and the Exhibit 3 survey, and thinks the reward is corroding the conversation: customers now ask about the ₹3,000 before they ask about generation. She has not said that her team's quality scores come from those same calls.

Kabir Dastur, product and design lead, Berlin. Wants the reward out of the sales conversation entirely, replaced by visible proof: signage, a neighbourhood generation map, an open house at a commissioned roof. He is on contract, has never sold a system in Saurashtra, and has not said that a European client is courting him.

Kumud Ranade, data science lead, Vancouver. Produced the holdout and states its confidence interval in every conversation, which nobody repeats back. She has not said that she considers the estimate weakly identified.

Komal Sethi, investment director, Singapore, board observer for the Series B fund. Benchmarks Kopal against portfolio companies in Vietnam and Spain and repeats that referral-led growth is what the fund underwrote. She has not said that its investment memo used the ₹7,658 figure, unadjusted, as evidence of a durable advantage.

7. Voices

"Every solar company in Gujarat has the same panel and the same subsidy. We have the neighbour. You are asking me to stop paying the neighbour." — Kunjan Dholakia, 30 September

"Nobody in that room has stood in a Kendra in Dhandhuka at month end. The ₹4,000 is not going to a neighbour, it is going to the shop that decided to quote Kopal instead of the other brand. Take it away and see what gets quoted." — Kedar Wagle, from Indore, 2 October

8. The options as Ketaki sees them

Hold and boost. Add a ₹2,000 festival top-up, taking the reward to ₹9,000 per commissioned referral. At the quarter's volume that is ₹131.22 lakh of payout plus ₹9.60 lakh of operations, or ₹140.82 lakh. It needs no notice period, since it raises the reward, and can be live in nine days. It also spends more on a channel of unestablished incrementality, in the only weeks when demand arrives anyway.

Cut and cap. Reduce to ₹3,000 for the referrer and ₹1,500 for the household, and cap the quarter at ₹60 lakh, which funds 1,333 commissioned referrals at ₹4,500 each. Khyati's preference. Clause 14 requires ninety days' notice, so a decision on 12 October takes effect on 10 January 2027, after the season it is meant to control, unless all forty-one partners consent in writing.

Move it into the channel. Pay the Kendra ₹5,000 per referred commissioning and let the partner decide what reaches the customer: ₹72.90 lakh plus operations, ₹82.50 lakh in all. It makes explicit what Kedar says already happens, and removes Kopal from a consumer payout under the DPDP flow. It also hands the customer relationship to a partner holding exclusivity until 2028.

Pay in service, not cash. Replace the referrer's ₹4,000 with three years of free cleaning and monitoring, which costs ₹1,150 a year. For the 58 per cent who would have bought an AMC, three free years forgo ₹4,860 of contribution; for the other 42 per cent, Kopal incurs ₹3,450 of cost. Weighted, the economic cost is ₹4,268 — above the ₹4,000 it replaces, with no cash leaving on commissioning day.

Stop, and buy proof instead. Close Kutumb Circle and redirect ₹111.66 lakh into discom camps, society drives, yard signage and open houses at commissioned roofs: Kabir's proposal, and the one that speaks to the 20.9 per cent in Exhibit 3 who decided on seeing panels go up.

Ketaki has arranged these as a spectrum from generous to austere, which is how the board will read them. What the arrangement hides is that all five argue about the size and recipient of a reward, and none touches Exhibit 6, where cycle time has stretched from 48 days to 63 and crews sit at 91 per cent. If a referral works partly because the neighbour's roof is visible, that 63-day gap is not a fulfilment problem but a marketing one, and every rupee spent generating orders lengthens the gap that generates referrals.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at 10:30 on Monday, 12 October 2026. Khyati has approved ₹460 lakh of growth spend for October to December against ₹442.86 lakh spent in the quarter just closed, so there is no room for both a festival boost and a new programme. Clause 14's ninety days binds any reduction; clause 9(c) bars Kopal's own canvassers from a partner taluka; the DPDP design rules out any return to uploaded contact lists. Fifty-eight crews at 91 per cent, with a seven-week training cycle, mean winter installed volume is close to fixed whatever demand does. Whatever Ketaki says on Monday will be quoted back to her in a January data room.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, state what the ₹7,658 figure measures and what it does not. What would have to be true for it to be the right number to manage the programme with?
  2. Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 give three pictures of what Kutumb Circle achieved. Reconcile them as far as you can, and say what you would measure to close the gap that remains.
  3. The holdout talukas were chosen by negotiation, not at random. In which direction does that bias the 8.6-point estimate, and how far would it have to run to reorder the options?
  4. Kedar argues the ₹4,000 is a channel incentive, not a customer reward. If he is right, which option is actually a price change to the partner network, and what does that imply about clause 14?
  5. Exhibit 6 is not about referral. Make the strongest case that it is the most important exhibit in the deck, then the strongest case that it is a distraction from Monday's decision.
  6. What should Ketaki do on Monday morning, and what should she say about the two numbers she cannot reconcile? Write the three sentences she opens with.

Figure B: the people around the decision, and the partners whose contracts bound it.

At twenty past midnight Ketaki closed the deck without changing the title slide, which still read "Kutumb Circle: scaling our cheapest channel". She had six exhibits, five options, two numbers that could not both be true, and nine hours.
case20v1-growth.referral:
Fasal Mitra Farm Inputs: The Referral That Cost More Than It Earned

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Fanindra Bhide sat in the glass-walled meeting room on the second floor of Fasal Mitra's head office in Warangal, with the quarterly referral report open on one screen and a blank slide titled "Recommendation" on the other. The board would meet on 13 October. Dussehra fell on 20 October, and the rabi sowing season, when Telangana and Andhra farmers buy most of their wheat, chickpea and maize inputs, would follow within weeks. Whatever Fanindra proposed had to be built, tested and live before the festival.

Fanindra, the company's head of growth, had one question to answer: should the referral programme that had brought in 30,000 new sign-ups last quarter be scrapped, repaired, or redesigned? The chief executive had said she would back any option that "pays for itself". Nobody had yet shown her that the current programme did.

2. Company background

Fasal Mitra Farm Inputs was founded in 2019 by Fulvanti Reddy, a former agronomy extension officer, and sells seed, fertiliser and crop-protection products to smallholder farmers in Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. Farmers order through an app or a WhatsApp catalogue, pay by UPI or on delivery, and receive goods at a village pickup point run by a local agri-retailer. In the last twelve months the company served 2,40,000 active farmers who placed an average of four orders each, roughly 9,60,000 orders at an average value of ₹3,000, a gross merchandise value of ₹288 crore. Contribution margin after product cost, freight and payment fees is about 18 per cent, or ₹540 per order.

The competition is crowded. DeHaat and BigHaat have deeper pockets, AgroStar is strong in Maharashtra, and cooperatives such as IFFCO sell directly through village societies. Farmers still trust the neighbour who farms the next plot more than any advertisement, which is why Fasal Mitra launched "Fulkari Rewards", a referral scheme, in early 2025. Any data handling in it follows the consent requirements of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and no phone contacts are uploaded; a farmer simply forwards a link on WhatsApp.

3. The situation

Fulkari Rewards paid ₹200 to the referrer and ₹200 to the new farmer as soon as the new farmer registered with a verified mobile number. The scheme was simple, cheap to build and popular. In July to September 2026, 15,000 referrers sent 1,20,000 invites, an average of eight each. Exhibit 1 follows those invites through to repeat purchase.

Exhibit 1 shows that payouts of ₹120 lakh bought only 9,000 first orders, or ₹1,333 each. Paid digital channels, which Fasal Mitra buys through Google and Meta, delivered a first order for ₹1,150. The referral channel, expected to be the cheapest, was the dearest.

Farheen Ansari, the data scientist working from Toronto, found the reason. A total of 6,300 registrations, 21 per cent of all, came from just 410 referrers who averaged about 15 sign-ups each, often on shared phones, and only 4 per cent of those farmers ever ordered, about 252 first orders. The remaining 23,700 registrations produced 8,748 first orders, a healthy 36.9 per cent. The scheme worked on genuine neighbours and leaked money to people gaming the sign-up bounty.

Fagun Trivedi, who runs field sales from Nagpur, sees the scheme differently. His retailers report that farmers like the ₹200 because it arrives as a UPI credit within minutes, and they dislike waiting for anything. Fanindra also heard from Firoz Pathan, the finance head in Pune, who asked bluntly whether ₹120 lakh a quarter could be justified when the money bought no more than paid channels did. Farheen, working five and a half hours behind Warangal, sent her analysis late at night with a caution: repeat behaviour came from a single quarter, so her projections were estimates.

4. The people

Fulvanti Reddy, chief executive, Warangal, wants growth that compounds. She built the company on word of mouth and will not abandon it, but she has told the board that she will not fund a programme that cannot show a positive return within a year.

Firoz Pathan, finance head, Pune, wants a defined budget ceiling and cash outflow he can forecast. He favours anything that ties payouts to margin.

Fagun Trivedi, head of field sales, Nagpur, wants farmers rewarded quickly. He fears that slow, conditional rewards will make retailers stop promoting the scheme in villages.

Farheen Ansari, data scientist, Toronto, wants the design measured properly and any change tested against a control group rather than launched everywhere at once.

5. Exhibits and the options

Fanindra and Farheen worked out three options over the weekend. Each assumes the same trigger of 1,20,000 invites, and Exhibit 2 compares the results Farheen expects. The paid-channel row spends the same ₹120 lakh at ₹1,150 per first order.

Option 1: pause referral and move the money to paid channels. It removes fraud and is simple to run, but at ₹1,150 a first order and only 2.0 orders a year each farmer barely repays acquisition, and Exhibit 3 shows a small loss. It also abandons Fasal Mitra's advantage of trust.

Option 2: pay ₹250 to the referrer and give the new farmer ₹250 off a first delivered order. Fake registrations earn nothing. Payout cost falls to ₹54 lakh and first orders rise to 10,800, the most volume of any option. The reward still lands quickly, which Fagun values. The weakness is that a first order can still be bought with a discount by a farmer who never returns.

Option 3: pay ₹150 on the first order and ₹450 to the referrer only when the new farmer places a second order within 90 days. It costs the least, ₹36 lakh, and creates the best farmers, but it produces 9,600 first orders, 1,200 fewer than Option 2, and the larger reward arrives after up to three months. Retailers may lose enthusiasm.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, why did the current scheme cost more per first order than paid channels, and what part of the gap did the 410 heavy referrers explain?
  2. Which of the three options changes the event that triggers payment, and why does that change the mix of farmers who join?
  3. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, compare Options 2 and 3 on volume, cost and first-year net contribution. Which assumption would have to be wrong for your ranking to reverse?
  4. What would you recommend to the board on 13 October, and how would you test it before Dussehra?

7. A note for the learner

A referral programme pays for itself when the reward buys a farmer who is worth more than the reward, and the framing that helps is unit economics per converted customer, not sign-ups or invites. The first discipline is to pay on an event that proves value. The current scheme paid on registration, which cost ₹1,333 per first order against contribution of ₹1,404 and left almost nothing. Each later option moves the trigger closer to what the company actually wants, a repeat buyer.

One defensible path is Option 3, launched to a controlled share of referrers first. Its first-year net of ₹114.34 lakh beats Option 2's ₹97.63 lakh by about ₹16.7 lakh, and it has the lowest cost per repeat farmer at ₹750. It also gives Firoz a lower, forecastable outlay of ₹36 lakh. The concerns are real: Fagun's worry about a slow reward is met by the ₹150 paid on the first order, and Farheen's caution is met by a holdout group of referrers who stay on the old scheme for six weeks. The main assumption to test is the 50 per cent repeat rate; if first orders fall well short of 9,600 during the test, the delayed reward is costing volume and Option 2 becomes the better choice. Fanindra should recommend Option 3 with that checkpoint stated in advance, and say plainly that the projections are estimates.

Referral Programme Design: A Referral That Pays for Itself

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation — Growth & Retention. Learning objective: design a referral programme whose reward economics are self-financing, not an act of faith.

A cheaper channel, or a more expensive one wearing a disguise

On the second Tuesday of November 2024, Rhea Kapoor, VP of Growth at Gehna Beauty, a Bengaluru-based direct-to-consumer skincare company with roughly nine lakh monthly active users on its app, sat across from the company's CFO in a glass-walled conference room on Indiranagar's 100 Feet Road with a single slide on the screen behind her. It showed one number: blended customer acquisition cost, trailing three months, had risen from ₹640 to ₹950. Eighteen months of Meta and Google auctions getting more crowded — Mamaearth, Sugar Cosmetics, and a dozen well-funded challengers bidding on the same keywords and the same lookalike audiences — had pushed paid acquisition to a point where the marketing budget, roughly ₹40 crore for the coming year, would buy meaningfully fewer new customers than it had the year before.

The CFO's question was not whether Gehna Beauty should try a referral programme. Two board members had already asked for one, citing Dropbox and Cred as reference points. His question was sharper: would this be a new source of paying customers, or a new discount aimed at customers who were going to buy anyway, dressed up in growth-team language so no one had to call it a discount? Rhea had seen referral programmes launched at two previous companies. Both had produced impressive-looking invite counts and unimpressive board conversations six months later, because nobody had built the arithmetic to answer the CFO's question before the button went live. She had eight weeks to bring back a specific proposal: reward structure, expected volume, and the number that mattered most — whether the fully-loaded cost of acquiring a customer through referral would be lower than what Gehna Beauty was already paying Meta, and by how much.

The idea, defined precisely

A referral programme is a structured mechanism that pays an existing customer — in cash, credit, or product — for successfully introducing a new customer, with the reward contingent on a defined outcome such as a signup or, better, a completed purchase. It is a formalisation of word-of-mouth: it does not create the underlying willingness of a customer to recommend a product, but it channels that willingness through a trackable, incentivised, and measurable mechanism instead of leaving it to chance. The idea has an identifiable lineage. PayPal's founding growth team, under Peter Thiel, Max Levchin and Elon Musk, is widely credited with popularising the modern referral programme in 1999–2000, paying $10 to a referring customer and $10 to the new signup — a scheme so aggressive it cost the company tens of millions of dollars but helped it reach critical mass before competitors could. Dropbox refined the model in 2008 under Drew Houston, replacing cash with free storage space for both sides, a reward that cost the company almost nothing in cash terms and was directly proportional to the product itself, and is credited with roughly a 60 percent lift in signups. The concept sits downstream of a related idea Gehna Beauty's growth team already knew: the viral coefficient, or the average number of new users each existing user brings in, which measures whether a product spreads on its own. Referral programme design is what a company does when it decides not to leave that coefficient to chance but to engineer it deliberately, by paying for the specific behaviour — sharing and successful conversion — that virality depends on.

The single sentence Rhea eventually wrote at the top of her board memo was this: a referral programme is a paid acquisition channel where the currency is a customer's trust instead of an ad platform's auction, and it only pays for itself when the reward it hands out costs less than the customer it buys is worth. That sentence sounds almost too simple to justify a slide deck, but nearly every referral programme that fails does so because someone skipped the second half of it.

How it actually works, mechanically

Stripped to its mechanics, a referral programme has six moving parts, and the parts practitioners most often leave implicit are the last two. First, a trigger moment: the point in the product experience where a customer is most likely to feel positively enough to share, typically right after a successful outcome — for Gehna Beauty, the moment a repeat customer's skin-tracking feature shows visible improvement, not the moment of first signup, when trust hasn't been earned yet. Second, a reward structure: single-sided, where only the advocate is paid, or double-sided, where both advocate and friend receive something, and the split between cash, credit, and product materially changes who responds. Third, the share mechanic itself — a unique trackable code or link, distributed via WhatsApp, SMS, or a native share sheet, since India's referral economics run overwhelmingly through WhatsApp rather than email. Fourth, attribution: the system of record that ties a new signup unambiguously to the advocate who sent it, typically via the code embedded in the link. Fifth — and this is the part most first-time programme owners never budget time for — fraud and abuse controls: without them, a rewards programme becomes an arbitrage opportunity the moment its economics become public, as coupon-aggregator sites and serial self-referrers discover it. Sixth, and the part that separates a programme finance will trust from one it won't, is reward timing and gating: whether the payout fires on signup (cheap to trigger, easy to game, rewards intent rather than value) or on a completed, paid first purchase (harder to game, aligned with the value the company actually received). Gehna Beauty's earlier informal referral scheme, run two years prior by a junior growth associate, had paid out on signup alone, and a retrospective audit found nearly a fifth of "referred" accounts had never placed an order.

The worked example: Gehna Beauty's proposal, line by line

Rhea built her case on a double-sided reward: ₹250 wallet credit to the advocate and a ₹250 discount off the friend's first order, contingent on a minimum order value of ₹999, with both rewards firing only after the friend's payment cleared. She modelled the funnel against Gehna Beauty's 1,00,000 monthly app users likely to see the referral prompt within a given month, using conversion assumptions calibrated from a two-week soft test run with 4,000 users the previous month.

In other words, the programme recovers its full cost within the customer's very first transaction. Every order after that, and Gehna Beauty's own data showed 3 orders per customer in a typical first year, is pure contribution margin: a 12-month LTV of roughly ₹2,520 in gross profit against a ₹599 CAC, an LTV:CAC ratio near 4.2:1.

The CFO's immediate counter-proposal was to richen the friend-side discount to ₹450 to push signups and purchases higher, on the theory that a bigger discount removes more friction. The richer reward still produced a programme cheaper than paid acquisition and still profitable over a year — but it no longer paid for itself within a single order, meaning Gehna Beauty would be carrying open exposure on every referred customer until that customer's second purchase actually happened, a bet on retention holding rather than a near-certainty banked on day one. Rhea's recommendation kept the original ₹250/₹250 structure specifically because of this difference: a self-liquidating first order is a materially safer position for a company already nervous about cash burn than a marginally higher volume bought with a longer, retention-dependent payback window.

Nine things a learner must become aware of

Referral CAC is not blended CAC, and the gap between them is where most self-deception lives

The 1,680 customers in Rhea's model are customers who redeemed a referral code, not necessarily customers who would not have found Gehna Beauty anyway. Some fraction of friends would have discovered the brand through search or Instagram within the quarter regardless of the invite; crediting the referral channel with their full value overstates the programme's efficiency. The only rigorous way to isolate the true incremental effect is a controlled holdout — switching referral off for a randomly selected slice of users or geographies and comparing organic conversion rates between the two groups. Without a holdout, a referral CAC number is a hypothesis, not a fact, however tidy the spreadsheet looks.

Single-sided and double-sided rewards optimise for different marginal actors

Paying only the advocate maximises invite volume from people who like free money; paying only the friend maximises conversion from price-sensitive prospects who need a nudge; paying both, as Gehna Beauty chose, balances the two but roughly doubles reward cost per successful referral. The choice is not merely a budget decision — it changes who in the funnel the programme is actually designed to move.

A referral programme is not affiliate or influencer marketing, and confusing them mis-prices both

An affiliate is paid to promote to strangers using reach they have built; a referrer is paid to vouch to people who already trust them personally. The conversion rates, fraud patterns, and appropriate reward sizes differ enormously between the two, and a programme designed with affiliate assumptions — percentage-of-sale commissions, for instance — will overpay relative to what a personal recommendation actually requires to happen.

The viral coefficient this topic depends on almost never exceeds one on its own

Outside of inherently communication-based products like messaging apps, the organic viral coefficient — new users generated per existing user without any incentive — is typically well below one, meaning the loop cannot sustain itself unaided. A referral programme's job is to lift that coefficient with a paid incentive; it is a growth-shaped acquisition channel, not proof that the product is inherently viral, and boards that treat a launched referral programme as evidence of virality are mistaking the subsidy for the phenomenon.

Reward economics cannot fix a retention problem, only amplify whatever is already there

If Gehna Beauty's underlying 90-day retention were poor, a referral programme would simply acquire more customers who also churn in 90 days, at a CAC that looks efficient right up until the LTV side of the ratio collapses. The programme measures and rewards acquisition; it says nothing about whether the product deserves the recommendation, and treating referral volume as a proxy for product health inverts cause and effect.

Fraud is not an edge case, it is a predictable response to a public incentive

The moment a ₹250/₹250 reward becomes known, it will appear on coupon-aggregator forums and be exploited by serial self-referrers using multiple phone numbers or family devices. Velocity checks on device ID, payment instrument, and delivery address, along with a cap on rewards per advocate per month, are not optional hardening — they are part of the base design, because unmitigated fraud inflates the "conversion" numbers in exactly the row of the funnel table that matters most.

Timing matters as much as reward size

Launching before a company has any organic word-of-mouth to amplify wastes the reward on customers who would have shared anyway at zero cost; launching well after competitors have normalised bigger rewards in the category forces a company to overpay just to be noticed. A simple pre-launch check — asking recent customers, via survey or a "would you recommend" prompt, whether they had already recommended the product unprompted — tells a team whether they are subsidising behaviour that already exists or genuinely creating new behaviour.

The programme decays, and the reward that worked at launch usually stops working within 12 to 18 months

Invite and conversion rates fall as the most enthusiastic, highest-affinity slice of the customer base's social graph gets exhausted first; the customers left to invite friends later are, on average, less enthusiastic and know fewer people who haven't already heard of the brand. A programme built to run indefinitely without revisiting reward size, trigger moments, or target segments will show a slow, easily-missed decline in the very ratios that justified it at launch.

Consumer, B2B, and marketplace: the same idea, three different machines

Gehna Beauty's design — a cash-like credit, a low-friction share link, a fast purchase cycle — suits a high-volume, low-ACV consumer product where the reward has to be small enough to be self-financing on a single order, exactly the constraint the worked example turned on. The picture changes sharply in B2B. Consider Gaurav FinServ, a Pune-based invoicing and ledger SaaS company selling to mid-market distributors: its customers are companies, not individuals, and the person who could refer a peer is often a finance manager who is not authorised to personally accept a cash reward for a purchase decision made on behalf of their employer, a pattern that edges uncomfortably close to a kickback and invites compliance scrutiny. Gaurav FinServ's referral mechanics instead run through account managers, offering the referring company additional product seats or service credits rather than cash to an individual, and the "share" moment is a customer-success conversation and a case study, not an in-app button — slower, higher-touch, and measured in a handful of referrals per quarter rather than thousands.

Marketplaces add a further wrinkle: which side gets rewarded. Girivan Stays, a homestay booking marketplace operating across hill-station towns, discovered that rewarding guests for referring other guests did little for the business, because guest demand was never the constraint — host supply was, particularly in newer destinations. Redirecting the same reward budget to hosts who referred other property owners moved the metric that was actually limiting growth, a reminder that in a two-sided marketplace the referral programme must be pointed at whichever side is scarce, not at whichever side is easiest to reach. Company stage matters too: an early-stage company often runs referral almost for free, funded by founder time and manual code-sharing in WhatsApp groups rather than cash, because the constraint at that stage is awareness, not cash discipline; a company at Gehna Beauty's scale must run the same idea as a governed, finance-reconciled channel with fraud infrastructure and holdout experiments, because at scale the absence of rigour is what turns a clever growth hack into a silent, recurring hole in the marketing budget.

Common mistakes, and the cheapest way to catch each one

The first mistake is declaring victory on invite volume while blended CAC across the whole company stays flat or rises. The symptom is a growth-team dashboard full of green numbers next to a finance dashboard showing no change; the underlying error is treating redeemed-code volume as incremental customers without a holdout to prove it. The cheapest diagnostic is a geo or cohort holdout run for even four to six weeks — expensive in the short term because it deliberately withholds a known-good lever from part of the base, but far cheaper than scaling an illusion.

The second mistake is measuring referral CAC on redeemed rewards only, ignoring the liability of credits earned but not yet spent and the amortised platform cost. The symptom is finance flagging a mysterious gap between the marketing team's reported CAC and the actual cash the finance ledger shows leaving the business; the fix is a fully-loaded CAC calculation, reconciled monthly with finance rather than reported unilaterally by growth.

The third mistake is rewarding the click or the signup instead of a paid, retained customer, which reliably produces a referred cohort that looks large but retains worse than any other acquisition channel. The symptom shows up two or three months after launch as a disappointing 90-day retention curve for the referred cohort specifically; the fix, as Rhea insisted on for Gehna Beauty, is gating reward on completed purchase from day one rather than retrofitting the gate after the damage to unit economics is already visible.

The fourth mistake is underestimating fraud until a spike in redemptions from a narrow cluster of devices or addresses forces an emergency shutdown of the programme, embarrassing the team that launched it. The cheapest diagnostic, run weekly rather than after the fact, is a simple concentration check — what share of redemptions come from the top hundred devices or IP ranges — which catches organised abuse long before it shows up as a finance anomaly.

What good looks like

A well-run referral programme, whether at Gehna Beauty's consumer scale or Gaurav FinServ's B2B one, shares a small set of habits regardless of industry. Reward is sized against a documented gross-profit calculation, not chosen by matching whatever a competitor announced on LinkedIn. Payout is gated on a paid, ideally retained, customer action, never on signup alone. A holdout or equivalent control group runs continuously, not as a one-time launch validation, so cannibalisation is a tracked metric rather than an assumption made once and never revisited. Fraud monitoring runs on a schedule, with a hard per-advocate cap, before any abuse pattern becomes visible in aggregate numbers. And the fully-loaded CAC, inclusive of engineering and ops amortisation, is reconciled with finance on the same monthly cadence as paid channels, sitting on the exact same dashboard so that a CFO can compare it to the Meta and Google line items without translation. None of these habits are exotic; the discipline is simply in doing all of them together, continuously, rather than doing the exciting part — the launch — and skipping the boring part that determines whether the programme still pays for itself a year later.

What Rhea decided

Rhea presented the ₹250/₹250 double-sided design to the board with three conditions attached, all drawn directly from the arithmetic: reward would fire only on a completed first purchase, a 20 percent holdout would run for the programme's first two full quarters to isolate true incrementality, and monthly spend would be capped at ₹15 lakh with a review gate before any increase to reward size. She declined the CFO's richer ₹450 friend-discount variant not because it was unprofitable — it wasn't — but because it traded a first-order payback, a near-certainty, for a second-order payback, a bet on retention the company had not yet stress-tested at that specific reward level. The board approved the pilot for January 2025. The next concept on Rhea's own reading list was cohort-based LTV modelling, because everything in her referral case ultimately rested on one assumption — 3 orders per customer in year one — that the programme itself does nothing to guarantee and that only a properly built cohort model could validate or contradict as real data came in.

Two questions worth sitting with.

If a referred friend would have discovered the brand within the quarter through organic search anyway, whose customer acquisition cost should the ₹500 reward be charged against — the referral channel that happened to reach them first, or the organic channel that would have reached them regardless? What changes about that answer if the true organic conversion rate is unknown until a holdout has run for months?

A programme can look self-financing on paper the moment a reward is redeemed, using only the first order's gross profit. How would you design the experiment, budget, and waiting period needed to know — not assume — that the referred cohort's second and third orders actually arrive at the same rate as every other cohort's do?

Referral Programme Design: The Marginal Rupee, Not the Average One

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation — Growth & Retention. Near-expert treatment. The question: can a referral programme pay for itself — and what exactly would count as evidence that it has?

1. Two rooms, one arithmetic

On 14 August 2025, in a windowless room on the eleventh floor of an office tower in Lower Parel, Meher Bakshi was defending a number she did not believe. Bakshi was VP of Growth at Trishala Money, a Mumbai consumer investing app with about 42 lakh registered users, 11 lakh of whom opened the app in a given month, and roughly 3.1 lakh of whom held a live systematic investment plan. The number on the screen was ₹1,480: the trailing blended cost of acquiring one funded account — not a download, not a KYC completion, but an account with money actually in it. Two years earlier it had been ₹760. Groww, Zerodha and a dozen well-capitalised challengers had made the discount-broking and direct-mutual-fund category one of the most contested advertising auctions in India, and Trishala Money's ₹58 crore annual growth budget was buying about 60 percent of the funded accounts it had bought in 2023.

The board's ask was not subtle. One director had circulated a note arguing that Trishala Money should "do what PayPal and Dropbox did" and let the customer base do the acquiring. Bakshi did not disagree with the instinct. What she disagreed with was the framing that had already taken hold in the room, which was that referral was a cheaper channel. Her own soft test, run in June across 40,000 users, had produced a headline referral cost of ₹500 per funded account against ₹1,480 paid — a number so flattering that she distrusted it on sight. Three things bothered her. Some fraction of those referred friends would have downloaded Trishala Money anyway; the reward had merely arrived first and taken the credit. The revenue side of an investing product is an annuity on assets under management, not a one-shot margin on an order, so "paying for itself" could not mean what it meant for a direct-to-consumer brand. And the ₹500 figure was an average, which told her nothing about what the next rupee of reward would buy. She had until the October board meeting to bring back a design, a budget, and — the part nobody had asked for — a measurement plan that could survive a hostile CFO.

Eleven hundred kilometres away and six months later, Anand Rangarajan was being asked a version of the same question with almost none of the same parameters. Rangarajan was Chief Product Officer at Trivikram Commerce Cloud, a Bengaluru company selling omnichannel retail software — catalogue, point of sale, inventory, storefront — to Indian mid-market chains with revenues between ₹50 crore and ₹500 crore. Trivikram had ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue across about 1,400 customers, an average contract value of ₹6.9 lakh, gross margin of 74 percent, and a sales motion built on outbound: a team of nineteen sales development representatives who sourced qualified opportunities at a fully-loaded cost of roughly ₹38,000 each, of which 22 percent eventually closed. New-logo CAC was about ₹2.9 lakh; payback ran to nineteen months.

In February 2026, Trivikram's CFO had proposed a customer referral programme paying ₹75,000 to any existing customer whose introduction closed. Rangarajan's head of demand generation, Ira Menon, had killed the idea in a single line — "we would never pay a ten percent commission to a customer" — and Rangarajan had let it die, then spent a weekend deciding she was wrong, for reasons that had nothing to do with generosity and everything to do with what ₹75,000 was being compared against. Trivikram's real question was not whether referral was cheap. It was whether referral could ever be large enough to matter, given that only a small minority of its customers were ever referenceable.

The two cases share one analytical spine, and it is the spine of this page. A referral programme is a purchase of customers at a price the company sets unilaterally, in a market where it cannot observe what it is actually buying. Everything difficult about the practice follows from that sentence: from the gap between average and marginal cost, from the impossibility of cheaply observing incrementality, from the fact that the reward is paid to someone who is not the buyer, and from the awkward truth that the behaviour being paid for already existed, for free, in some unknown quantity, before the programme launched.

2. The idea, its lineage, and the four schools that disagree about it

A referral programme is a firm-offered, contingent incentive paid to an existing customer for the verified introduction of a new customer, where the contingency is defined on an outcome the firm values. Three words in that definition do real work. Firm-offered distinguishes it from the interpersonal incentives people already give each other — the social credit of good advice — which the programme sits on top of and can disturb. Contingent locates the entire design problem: on what, exactly, and at what lag. And verified imports an attribution system, which is where most of the engineering cost and all of the fraud exposure live.

The intellectual history runs older than the growth-team era. Frank Bass's 1969 diffusion model separated adoption driven by external influence — advertising, the coefficient conventionally written p — from adoption driven by internal influence, word of mouth from those who have already adopted, written q. Bass gave marketers a vocabulary for the idea that a product's growth curve has an endogenous component, but no lever for moving it. The lever arrived commercially in 1999–2000, when PayPal paid new users and their referrers ten dollars each and bought its way to a critical mass of network density ahead of competitors, stepping the bonus down to five and then two dollars as the network's own gravity took over. That step-down is the more instructive half of the story and is usually omitted when the case is retold: the programme was designed from the start as a decaying subsidy on a coefficient, not as a permanent channel. Dropbox's 2008 double-sided storage reward — free gigabytes to both sides, capped — added the insight that the reward's currency matters as much as its size, because storage cost Dropbox almost nothing at the margin and selected for users who valued exactly the thing the product did. Airbnb's 2014 rebuild added a third: when the team tested framings, the altruistic construction ("give your friend ₹2,000 of travel") outperformed the self-interested one, which is a finding about the psychology of the referrer, not about the size of the pot.

Academic work arrived roughly in parallel and is more sceptical than the practitioner literature. Biyalogorsky, Gerstner and Libai's 2001 treatment of optimal reward programmes set the problem up as a pricing problem with two instruments — price and bounty — and showed that the optimum depends on customer delight thresholds rather than on referral volume. Kornish and Li's 2010 analysis produced the result most practitioners find counter-intuitive and most experts consider foundational: if a referrer partly internalises the friend's welfare, a larger bounty can reduce referrals, because the referrer reads a rich bounty as evidence that the product is hard to sell, and because accepting payment for a recommendation contaminates the recommendation's meaning. Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte's 2011 study of a German bank found referred customers had higher margins and better retention than matched non-referred customers, with the premium decaying but persisting for about three years — a result that has been used to justify very large bounties and that later work by Van den Bulte and colleagues partly deflated by decomposing the premium into homophily (advocates refer people like themselves, and good customers know good customers) and signalling (the vouch itself changes behaviour).

From this history four schools have crystallised. They are not caricatures; each has serious practitioners and each would sign a proposition the others would not.

The engineered-loop school descends from the PayPal–Dropbox lineage and the growth-engineering tradition. It holds that word of mouth is an instrumentable system: a trigger, a share surface, an attribution key, a reward, a fraud gate, each independently testable. It will sign: reward size, timing and framing are empirical parameters and the correct value is whatever a controlled test says it is. It will not sign: a large and growing referral volume is evidence that the product is loved, because it knows perfectly well that volume is a function of the subsidy.

The brand and mental-availability school, associated with the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition and with the Net Promoter lineage in a different register, holds that recommendation is an output of satisfaction and salience, and that metering it with money buys the wrong customers while degrading the signal you most need. It will sign: measure the unincentivised recommendation rate, and treat a falling one as a product problem no bounty can fix. It will not sign: a referral programme raises the long-run growth rate of the brand; at best, it argues, the programme pulls forward acquisitions that penetration and availability would have delivered anyway.

The incentive-design school treats the bounty as a price and looks for an interior optimum. It will sign: there exists a reward above which referrals fall, and it can be below the reward that maximises reported volume. It will not sign: the response of referrals to reward is monotone increasing, which is exactly the assumption embedded in almost every growth-team reward ladder ever built.

The incrementality school — the econometric sceptics, whose canonical texts are Blake, Nosko and Tadelis on paid search and Lewis and Rao on the unfavourable statistics of measuring advertising returns — holds that reported channel efficiency is contaminated by selection until an experiment says otherwise, and further that the experiments required are often larger than firms can run. It will sign: an unmeasured channel's incremental return should be treated as unknown, and the width of that uncertainty should drive the budget. It will not sign: because we cannot measure it, we should assume it works — nor, in its honest form, the reverse.

Bakshi's working note to herself, August 2025: "Every school in the room agrees the programme will produce redemptions. They disagree about what a redemption is evidence of. That is the whole argument."

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic experts actually run

Begin with the formalism, because it disciplines the rest. Let i be invites sent per existing user per cycle and c the probability an invite converts to a new activated user. Their product is the referral coefficient K = i × c. For K below one, a seed cohort of N users eventually produces N / (1 − K) total users through all generations; the cycle time t determines how quickly. Two teams with identical K of 0.4 but cycle times of four days and forty days are not running the same programme in any operational sense: at a fixed calendar horizon the fast loop compounds ten times more often, which is why an expert asks about time-to-second-invite before asking about coefficient.

The first place where competent practice diverges from expert practice is the treatment of amplification in the cost calculation. Trishala Money's soft test produced, among referred users, a rewarded referral coefficient of 0.28 and an unrewarded organic coefficient of 0.12 — friends who arrived through a forwarded screenshot, a WhatsApp group mention or a search for the app name with no code attached. The intuitive move, which Bakshi's analyst made in the first draft, was to take the fully-loaded cost per rewarded referral and divide it by the amplification factor 1/(1 − 0.40) = 1.667, producing a flattering "amplification-adjusted CAC" of ₹445 against ₹741.

That calculation is wrong, and understanding why is the single most useful mechanical insight in the topic. Amplification reduces cost per customer only for generations you do not pay for. Every second-generation user who arrives with a code in hand triggers another ₹500 of reward; those descendants are not free, they are simply the next purchase. Only the organic coefficient earns the discount. Correctly: each rewarded customer yields 1/(1 − 0.12) = 1.136 total customers, so the effective cost is ₹741 ÷ 1.136 = ₹652. The full generational accounting gives the same answer: from one seed, the tree contains 1/(1 − 0.40) = 1.667 customers, of whom 1.467 are rewarded; 1.467 × ₹741 = ₹1,087 spread over 1.667 customers is ₹652 per customer. A twelve percent discount, not a forty percent one.

The second divergence concerns average versus marginal cost, and it is where most programmes quietly destroy value while reporting success. Bakshi ran a randomised reward-size test across four cells in July, holding trigger, copy and gating constant and varying only the amount. The response was concave, as reward responses almost always are: a threshold below which nothing happens, a steep middle, and a plateau where the marginal referrer has already been bought.

Experts respond to this in one of three ways, and the choice is a genuine judgement call. Some run a geo or cluster-randomised holdout across pin-code groups, accepting that clustering inflates the required sample further but buying cleaner spillover control. Some run switchback designs, turning the prompt on and off across weeks, which is cheap but confounded by seasonality in a category where investing flows follow salary and tax cycles. And some — this is the position Bakshi eventually took — accept the wide interval and set policy on its lower bound, budgeting as if incrementality were at the pessimistic end and treating any outperformance as a windfall rather than a plan.

Two further mechanical steps are routinely left implicit. The first is gating design, which is not a binary between signup and purchase but a ladder of increasingly expensive-to-fake events: install, KYC, first debit, first debit that survives a sixty-day cooling window without redemption. Each rung up the ladder cuts fraud and adverse selection, and each rung adds lag between the advocate's effort and the reward, which is precisely what suppresses participation. Bakshi's compromise — reward released on first successful SIP debit plus a sixty-day hold — cost roughly 9 percent of participation against immediate-on-KYC release and removed about 80 percent of the abuse signature. The second is liability and revenue recognition. Wallet credit is not marketing expense; under Ind AS 115 a credit that confers a material right on a customer is typically a separate performance obligation, so the advocate's ₹250 defers revenue rather than consuming budget, and the friend's ₹250 may be contra-revenue rather than cost. Where that argument lands determines reported gross margin, reported CAC, and whether the growth team's dashboard and the finance ledger can ever be reconciled. Programmes that skip this conversation before launch discover it in the audit.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions, each falsifiable, each applied to both protagonists.

Claim one: the product already produces unincentivised recommendation at a measurable rate. The test is not a survey question but a log: count new users who arrive by direct navigation or branded search with a prior-user contact in their device graph, or simply measure the organic coefficient the way Bakshi did, at 0.12. Trishala Money passes. Trivikram passes in an attenuated form — Menon's team could name eleven deals in three years that had been sourced by a customer introduction, all unrewarded. Where the organic coefficient is indistinguishable from zero, a bounty does not amplify word of mouth, it manufactures a discount and calls it word of mouth.

Claim two: contribution margin over a horizon the firm can finance exceeds fully-loaded reward cost. Trishala Money's funded account contributes roughly ₹620 in year one, ₹1,180 in year two and ₹1,590 in year three at 78 percent annual retention — about ₹2,510 over three years. Against a fully-loaded ₹741 that is 3.4:1, against paid acquisition's ₹1,480 it is 1.7:1. Note what this does not say: unlike a fast-moving consumer product, the referral does not pay for itself inside the first transaction. It pays for itself in about twelve months. That is a financing question, not a marketing one, and the CFO is the right person to answer it.

Claim three: the advocate population is large enough that saturation is years away, not quarters. Here the two protagonists diverge sharply, and it is the most consequential difference between them. Trishala Money has 11 lakh monthly actives; even at a 3.2 percent monthly share rate the eligible pool renews faster than it depletes. Trivikram has 1,400 customers, of whom Menon estimated 9 percent were genuinely referenceable — live for more than four quarters, above a health-score threshold, with a named champion still in post. That is 126 advocates, producing perhaps 0.6 introductions each per year: 76 referrals, 31 wins at the referred close rate of 41 percent, roughly ₹2.1 crore of new ARR against a ₹34 crore new-ARR plan. Trivikram's referral programme cannot be a growth engine. It can only be a margin programme. Recognising that before launch, rather than after two quarters of disappointed board slides, is the difference between a competent and an expert answer.

Claim four: attribution is cheap enough relative to deal size that verification does not consume the saving. Trishala Money verifies with a code and a device graph at negligible marginal cost. Trivikram must verify a human claim — "I introduced you to this retailer" — against a pipeline that may already have contained the account, which is why every mature B2B programme runs a deal-registration window and why disputes over it consume more of the programme owner's time than any other activity.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When the product is bought once in a lifetime or once per household, the advocate's remaining useful graph is near-empty and the programme buys nothing but fraud. When the category is in a bounty arms race, referral becomes an undifferentiated price cut that every competitor matches within a quarter, leaving relative share unchanged and every player's margin lower — at which point the correct question is no longer "does it pay for itself" but "what does it cost to be the only firm without one". And when the firm's retention is weak, referral is an accelerant on a leaking tank: it acquires more of a cohort that churns, at a CAC that looks excellent right until the LTV denominator arrives.

In Indian financial services, the boundary between an introduction and a solicitation carries real consequences: rewards that scale with the amount invested look materially different to a regulator than a flat ₹250 paid for an account opening, and any copy implying advice can move a consumer programme into territory that assumes registration the firm does not hold. Trishala Money's compliance counsel imposed two conditions on Bakshi before any test ran: the reward could not vary with ticket size, and the advocate's share message could not contain a return figure. Both cost participation. Both were correct.

The AI-native case inverts the Dropbox lesson so thoroughly that quoting Dropbox in an AI product's referral review should be treated as a warning sign. Dropbox's storage had near-zero marginal cost and its heaviest users were its most valuable. Tokens are not storage. When Trishala Money's product team proposed rewarding referrals with free queries on the Trishala Advisor assistant, the growth analytics showed the obvious: query-hungry users were disproportionately the ones who never funded an account, so the reward would have been a direct transfer of variable cost to the least monetisable segment, with an abuse surface — bulk identity creation for free inference — that had no analogue in 2008.

The organisational seams matter as much as the product ones. In every large company that runs a referral programme well, four functions hold veto power over a design that growth nominally owns. Finance determines whether the reward is expense or contra-revenue and therefore what CAC and gross margin get reported. Risk owns the fraud rules and, crucially, the false-positive rate: a velocity rule tight enough to stop a ring will also block the power-advocate cohort that produces the programme's best volume. Legal owns the terms and the copy, and in India also owns exposure to consumer-protection guidance on dark patterns, which bears directly on countdown timers, pre-ticked consents and the "false urgency" constructions that referral surfaces attract. Customer support absorbs the disputes, which arrive at a rate roughly proportional to gating strictness. Programmes that fail organisationally usually fail because growth shipped first and negotiated with these four afterwards, at which point every negotiation is conducted under the threat of switching off something customers can already see.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The inframarginal transfer. Raising a bounty pays the increase to everyone who would have referred at the old level. The tell-tale sign is a reward-increase proposal justified by a projected volume lift with no marginal-cost column; the obvious reading is that a bigger bounty buys more customers, which is true and irrelevant, because the question is what the next customer costs. An expert asks for Table 1's fifth column before reading the second.

K is a distribution, not a mean. Referral volume is reliably power-law: at Trishala Money the top 1.2 percent of advocates produced 38 percent of funded referrals. The tell-tale sign is a growth plan built on an average coefficient applied uniformly across the base. The obvious reading — that the programme is broadly popular — is wrong twice over: planning on the mean overstates reach into the long tail, and the same concentration statistic is the primary fraud signal, which means the best segment and the abuse ring look identical in the first pass of the data and must be separated by graph structure, not by volume.

Cycle time beats coefficient. A coefficient of 0.35 with an eight-day loop compounds faster over a quarter than 0.6 with a fifty-day loop. The tell-tale sign is a team that can quote K to two decimals and cannot quote median days from reward receipt to next share. The obvious reading treats K as the growth rate; it is only half of it.

The referred-customer premium is mostly selection. Referred cohorts genuinely retain better, but decompose the premium and most of it is homophily — good customers know good customers — rather than any magic in the vouch. The tell-tale sign is a business case that justifies a large bounty by citing the referred cohort's superior LTV without matching on advocate quality. The obvious reading, that the referral caused the quality, licenses overpayment; the correct reading is that a large part of that value would have been available through any channel that reached the same social stratum.

Crowding out is real and arrives quietly. Paying for a behaviour that people were performing for social reasons can reduce the behaviour, a finding with a long lineage from Titmuss on blood donation to Gneezy and Rustichini on fines. In referral, the mechanism is specific: an unpaid recommendation carries information — I thought of you — that a paid one does not, and some advocates stop rather than accept the reframing. The tell-tale sign is a dip in direct and branded-search signups in the treated geography in the four weeks after launch, exactly when referral redemptions are climbing. The obvious reading is seasonality. The diagnostic is whether the dip is absent in the holdout.

Reward type dominates reward size at the bottom of the ladder. Ryu and Feick's work on tie strength points the same way as Kornish and Li's: for strong ties, product credit and in-kind rewards preserve the sincerity of the recommendation while cash converts the advocate into a salesperson. The tell-tale sign is a team that has A/B tested four amounts and zero currencies. The obvious reading is that money is fungible and ₹250 is ₹250; the experimental record says the same ₹250 in wallet credit, in a charitable donation, or in cash produces materially different sharing rates among different tie strengths.

Graph exhaustion is a stock problem masquerading as a rate problem. Every advocate holds a finite inventory of uninvited, plausible contacts, and the programme spends it. The tell-tale sign is diagnostic and precise: invites sent per advocate holds steady while conversion per invite declines. The obvious reading is creative fatigue, and teams respond by rewriting the share copy, which does nothing. The correct response is to widen the advocate base, lengthen the cycle, or accept a lower steady state.

The advocate side is a retention instrument. The act of recommending increases the recommender's own commitment; advocates who share, even when the invite fails to convert, retain measurably better than matched non-sharers. The tell-tale sign is a business case that counts only acquired customers. The obvious reading treats the advocate reward as pure cost; on a full accounting, part of it is a retention expense that would otherwise be spent through a loyalty programme with worse targeting.

Attribution windows create double-counting, and nobody notices because both dashboards are green. A friend clicks a referral link, does not convert, returns eleven days later through a branded search ad, and is claimed by both channels. The tell-tale sign is arithmetic: the sum of channel-attributed new customers exceeds total new customers. The obvious reading is that attribution is "directionally fine"; the consequence is that the referral programme's reported CAC and the paid team's reported CAC are both understated, and the company's blended CAC — the only number that cannot lie — stubbornly refuses to fall.

Breakage is a liability, not a saving. Unredeemed wallet credit accumulates, and growth teams routinely present the unredeemed balance as evidence that the programme costs less than modelled. The tell-tale sign is a rising "earned but unspent" line described in a growth review as efficiency. The obvious reading is wrong because the obligation exists until it expires, the expiry terms may themselves be contested, and — the second-order effect — high breakage usually means the reward is failing to create the repeat engagement that justified the double-sided structure in the first place.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products with short purchase cycles and large bases, referral behaves most like the textbook: high volume, small rewards, fast loops, fraud as an industrial-scale problem, and measurement limited by base rates rather than by sample. In B2B and enterprise, almost every parameter inverts, and the most important inversion is what the reward is benchmarked against. Menon's objection — "a ten percent commission" — compared ₹75,000 against the ₹6.9 lakh contract. That is the wrong denominator. A referral does not replace the sale; the account executive still runs the cycle. It replaces sourcing.

Platforms and marketplaces add the balance constraint — the bounty must point at the scarce side and, because liquidity is local, must usually be geo-fenced rather than run nationally. Where the differences are not real, it is worth saying so plainly: the gating ladder, the inframarginal arithmetic, the incrementality problem and the fraud response are identical across all of them. Practitioners often assume their context is exotic when only the parameters differ.

Stage matters in one direction that is frequently misread. Early-stage firms are told they are too small for referral; in fact a seed-stage company can run the mechanism almost free, through founder-distributed codes in WhatsApp communities, because its constraint is awareness and its measurement obligations are near zero. What it cannot do is learn anything generalisable from the result, because at that volume every estimate is noise. Scale reverses both: the arithmetic becomes knowable and the absence of governance becomes expensive.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Trishala Money, consumer, succeeded with a caveat. Launched November 2025 at ₹250 per side, gated on first successful SIP debit plus a sixty-day hold, capped at five rewards per advocate per quarter, with a 12 percent user-level holdout. Over the first two quarters: 8,940 funded referred accounts, reward cost ₹44.7 lakh, fully-loaded cost ₹66.2 lakh, or ₹741 per account. The holdout showed the treated arm at 0.44 percent versus control at 0.36 percent — a point estimate implying about 18 percent cannibalisation, with a confidence interval running from 4 to 31 percent. Bakshi budgeted the following year on the 31 percent figure, which raised the true incremental cost to ₹1,074 and still beat ₹1,480. The caveat: the marginal-cost policy she wrote into the programme charter — no reward increase whose projected marginal cost exceeds 0.8 times paid CAC — was tested in month five when a competitor launched a richer offer, and it held only because the CFO had co-signed it in writing.

Trivikram Commerce Cloud, B2B, succeeded as something other than what was proposed. Approved April 2026 with the reward restructured from cash to a ₹75,000 service credit against the referring company's next invoice — a change driven not by generosity but by tax and governance. A cash benefit to a business customer raises withholding questions under Section 194R and, more practically, most of Trivikram's mid-market customers have vendor codes forbidding personal gifts to employees involved in purchasing. The credit is paid to the entity; the individual champion receives a non-transferable benefit — a certification, a place on the customer advisory board — which their employer can approve without a policy exception. First-year result: 71 referrals registered, 46 accepted after deal-registration checks, 19 closed-won, ₹1.34 crore of new ARR at a reward cost of ₹14.25 lakh. Below Rangarajan's own ceiling estimate, and unambiguously the cheapest ARR in the company.

Trishna Home Services, marketplace, failed and recovered. In September 2024 the Pune-based home-services marketplace launched a ₹200-per-side customer referral on first booking, on the reasoning that more customers is always good. Demand was never the constraint. In Trishna's newer pin codes the job-fill rate was 61 percent; the programme drove booking volume up 23 percent in seven months at a reward cost of ₹1.9 crore, and fill rate fell to 54 percent as demand outran available professionals. Average rating dropped, refunds rose, and a concentration audit found that 11 percent of redemptions in two pin codes traced to a small cluster of recycled SIMs settling to a shared UPI handle. The programme was suspended in April 2025.

The recovery is the instructive part, because it was not a fix to the programme but a reversal of its direction. Trishna's growth lead, Ipsita Deb, moved the budget to the supply side: ₹1,500 to a professional who referred another professional, paid in two tranches — ₹600 on the referred professional's tenth completed job, ₹900 on the fortieth — with a 4.6-star quality gate and geo-restriction to 43 supply-deficient pin codes. Over the following nine months, 2,870 professionals were onboarded through referral at a fully-loaded ₹1,840 against ₹4,300 through field recruiters, with 90-day retention of 71 percent versus 52 percent for recruiter-sourced supply. Fill rate recovered to 78 percent. The retention gap is homophily again — professionals refer from the same neighbourhood and the same trade network, and the vouch creates a form of accountability a recruiter cannot manufacture. The lesson Deb drew, and repeated in every subsequent planning cycle, was that the failure had not been in reward size, gating or fraud control. It had been in pointing a growth instrument at a variable that was not constraining growth.
