10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether to pay at all. The engineered-loop position holds that unincentivised word of mouth is a coefficient below one in almost every category outside communications, that a subsidy is the only available lever, and that PayPal's step-down shows the subsidy can be withdrawn once density is achieved. The brand position holds that the recommendation rate is a function of satisfaction and mental availability, that paying for it corrupts a diagnostic signal the firm badly needs, and that the observed lift is mostly pulled-forward demand. Each rests on different evidence: the first on programme-level before-and-after data, the second on long-run penetration studies in mature categories. The first would be wrong if well-run holdouts consistently showed incrementality near zero across categories; the second would be wrong if firms that withdrew mature programmes saw no compensating recovery in organic acquisition. Both experiments are run rarely, and the results are not public.

Whether reward response is monotone. Practitioners overwhelmingly behave as though more money means more referrals up to a budget limit. The incentive-design literature says a sufficiently large bounty can signal desperation and contaminate the vouch, producing an interior optimum below the volume-maximising level. The practitioner reply is that the theoretical non-monotonicity occurs at bounty levels no firm would rationally offer, so the result is correct and irrelevant. The steelman for theory: the relevant range is not the bounty in rupees but the bounty relative to price. A ₹600 bounty on a ₹999 product is a very different social object from ₹600 on a ₹60,000 one, and category evidence of declining share rates at high reward-to-price ratios does exist. What would settle it is a reward ladder extended deliberately past the plateau, which almost nobody runs because it looks like deliberately wasting money.

Whether the referred-customer premium justifies a premium bounty. One camp cites the bank study and its multi-year persistence of higher margin and retention; the other cites the homophily decomposition and argues that most of the premium is selection available by other means. Practically, the disagreement determines whether a firm may pay more for a referred customer than for a paid one. The first camp would be wrong if advocate-matched controls consistently closed the gap, as Fig. 3 suggests they largely do at Trishala Money; the second would be wrong if the residual signalling effect proved large in categories with high perceived risk — financial services, healthcare, education — where a vouch carries more information than in commodity retail. There is reasonable evidence that the residual is bigger in exactly those categories, which means both camps may be right about different products and neither has a general answer.

Whether measurement rigour is worth its cost. The incrementality school's own literature contains the argument against it: the experiments needed to measure marketing returns precisely are often larger than the budgets at stake, which is Lewis and Rao's uncomfortable conclusion. The pragmatist position is that a programme costing ₹66 lakh a year does not justify parking 18 percent of the user base in a control cell for two quarters, and that a decision rule based on a wide interval's lower bound is good enough. The rigorist replies that the cost of the holdout is paid once while the cost of a wrong belief compounds annually. Bakshi's choice — run the holdout, but design the policy so that the answer changes the budget rather than the go/no-go — is a common compromise, and it is a compromise, not a resolution.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied referral design can describe the double-sided reward, the gating ladder and the viral coefficient. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They ask for the marginal-cost column before the average one, and they will not approve a reward increase without it. They treat the reported referral CAC as a hypothesis with a confidence interval attached and speak about it that way in front of a board, which is uncomfortable and is the whole point. They locate the constraint before pointing the instrument: Deb's reversal at Trishna Home Services is the canonical example, and the expert's version of that move happens before ₹1.9 crore is spent, not after. And they negotiate the finance, risk, legal and support positions before launch, because they know the programme's real constraint is rarely the reward budget and frequently the false-positive rate on a fraud rule or the question of whether wallet credit is expense or contra-revenue.

There is a fifth, subtler tell. Experts are comfortable concluding that a referral programme should exist but should be small — that it is a margin improvement rather than a growth engine, as at Trivikram — and they say so in the same meeting where they propose it. Practitioners who have only studied the topic tend to argue for the programme's importance in proportion to their enthusiasm for it, which is precisely the sentiment that produced the board note Bakshi had to answer in August.

12. What each of them decided

Bakshi presented in October 2025 and got approval for ₹250 per side, not the ₹400 the growth plan had originally modelled, on the explicit basis that marginal cost crossed the paid benchmark at about ₹350. She attached four conditions: reward on first successful SIP debit plus sixty days; five rewards per advocate per quarter; a 12 percent holdout for two quarters with the budget set on the interval's pessimistic end; and a written marginal-cost ceiling of 0.8 times paid CAC that only the CFO could waive. She also conceded, in the memo, the thing the board did not want to hear — that at ₹66 lakh a year the programme would contribute perhaps 9 percent of new funded accounts, and that the paid-acquisition problem the board had asked her to solve remained unsolved.

Rangarajan approved Trivikram's programme in April 2026 with the reward converted to a service credit, a 45-day deal-registration window to protect the existing reseller channel from routing deals through the cheaper path, and an explicit statement in the board pack that the programme's realistic ceiling was six percent of the new-ARR plan. He funded it by not hiring the twentieth sales development representative — a trade he made visible deliberately, so that the programme would be judged against the alternative it actually displaced rather than against nothing.

Discussion questions.

1. Bakshi budgeted on the pessimistic end of a confidence interval running from 4 to 31 percent cannibalisation. Under what circumstances is that prudence, and under what circumstances is it a way of avoiding a measurement she should have insisted on being able to make? What would you have required before approving the programme?

2. Trivikram's ₹75,000 bounty is 10.9 percent of contract value and 43 percent of sourcing cost per win. Which comparison should govern the decision, and what changes if the referred deals would have closed anyway through the outbound motion six months later?

3. Deb reversed the direction of Trishna Home Services' programme rather than repairing it. Identify the earliest moment in the original design review at which the supply constraint should have been visible, and name the specific artefact — a metric, a table, a question — whose absence allowed ₹1.9 crore to be spent before it was.

13. Going deeper

  1. Virality and the viral coefficient — the parent concept. Referral programmes are the engineered case of a coefficient that is otherwise given; understanding the unincentivised baseline is what tells you whether a bounty is amplifying something or manufacturing it.
  2. Growth loops vs funnels — referral is the clearest loop in most products, and the loop framing is what surfaces cycle time, the variable this page argues matters more than the coefficient.
  3. Building a growth model — the discipline that turns Table 1 into a plan; a growth model is where marginal cost, saturation and cannibalisation assumptions have to be written down and can therefore be argued with.
  4. Acquisition channels and economics — referral only means something against a benchmark; the comparison to paid, organic and sales-led channel economics is the entire basis of the "pays for itself" claim.
  5. Activation and onboarding optimisation — the referred friend's conversion rate is mostly an activation problem, not a reward problem, and the cheapest lever in most referral programmes lives here rather than in the bounty.
  6. Engagement loops and habit — the trigger moment depends on knowing when a user has actually received value; without an engagement model the share prompt is placed by guesswork.
  7. Retention strategy — the denominator of every calculation on this page. Referral amplifies whatever retention already exists, which makes retention strategy the prerequisite rather than the sequel.
